1950
Have you ever wondered
what an advanced alien
civilization would see
if they aimed a
super-telescope at Earth
right now?
Imagine an alien astronomer
sitting on a planet
on the opposite side
of our Milky Way galaxy.
They would not see
our cities, our glowing
screens, or the satellites
orbiting overhead.
In fact, they would
have no idea our
modern society even exists.
Light travels at an
incredible three hundred
thousand kilometers per
second, but our galaxy
is so enormous that
it takes light roughly
one hundred thousand years
to travel from one
side to the other.
Human beings have only
been broadcasting radio
signals into space for
about a single century.
That means our technological
footprint is a tiny
bubble only a couple
of hundred light-years across.
For scale, the nearest
star beyond the sun
is more than four
light-years away, and
Voyager 1, the most
distant spacecraft we have
ever launched, would need
roughly seventy thousand
years to get there.
To anyone watching from
across the galaxy,
the light reaching their
telescope left Earth about
one hundred thousand years
ago, during the last ice age.
If they could make
out any detail at
all, they would find
a world of glacial
ice, woolly mammoths on
the tundra, and early
humans surviving with stone
tools.
The eerie silence of
deep space does not
prove the cosmos is empty.
It may simply mean
that space is terrifyingly
large, and that we
have only been whispering
into the dark for
a fraction of a second.
This puzzle has a
name, the Fermi Paradox,
after the physicist Enrico
Fermi, who is said
to have asked over
lunch in 1950,
where is everybody?
Distance and time may
be a big part
of the answer.
Compress the whole history
of the universe into
one calendar year,
and all of recorded
human history fits into
the last ten seconds
or so before midnight
on December thirty-first.
If you walked through
an endless forest at
night and heard no
human voices, you would
not assume the rest
of the planet was dead.
You would assume that
people were simply too
far away to hear.

to explore the mind-bending
reality of cosmic distance,
and what it means
for the search for life.
